passages.t: Tear open the heavens and come down
passages.happening:
The prayer goes on. ‘If only You would rend the heavens and come down, so that mountains would quake at Your presence’ (verse 1), as fire makes water boil, so that the nations would tremble (verse 2). ‘When You did awesome works that we did not expect, You came down, and the mountains trembled at Your presence’ (verse 3).

‘From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him’ (verse 4).

Then confession. ‘You welcome those who gladly do right, who remember Your ways’ (verse 5). But God was angry, because they sinned. ‘How can we be saved if we remain in our sins?’ (verse 5). ‘Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags’ (verse 6). ‘We all wither like a leaf, and our iniquities carry us away like the wind’ (verse 6). No one calls on God's name or takes hold of him, because he has hidden his face and handed them over to their own iniquity (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the second half of the lament that began at 63:7. There the people remembered the exodus and asked where the God of Moses had gone. Here they ask him to come back in person, with the power he showed at Sinai.

The prayer reaches back to the times God came down: Sinai wrapped in fire, smoke and trembling, and the old poems of God coming in storm. The ancient sky was pictured as a solid dome, so to tear it open was a vivid way to ask God to break into the world. The word for rend is the word for tearing clothes in grief.

The confession in verse 6 uses the language of the purity laws. Unclean was a ritual state that kept a person from worship until cleansing. The phrase filthy rags is, in Hebrew, a cloth stained by a woman's monthly blood, which the law treated as ritually unclean. The prayer does not say bodies are shameful. It says that even the people's best religious deeds, done while their hearts were turned from God, could not make them fit to come before him.

In Hebrew Bibles, the verse English Bibles call 64:1 is the last line of chapter 63, so the Hebrew numbering runs one lower. The words are the same.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 4 as he writes of God's wisdom: ‘No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him’ (1 Corinthians 2:9). At Sinai ‘the whole mountain quaked violently’ (Exodus 19:18).
passages.hard:
Does verse 6 mean that every good deed people do is worthless to God?

The verse is often quoted to say that all human goodness is filthy in God's sight, and that needs care. In context the speakers are God's own people confessing that they have sinned, stopped calling on him, and been handed over to their iniquity. Their righteous acts, the religious observances they might point to, cannot cleanse them or earn God's favor while their hearts are turned away. Verse 5 also says that God welcomes those who gladly do right, so the chapter does not say doing right means nothing to him.

Christian traditions draw on the verse in different ways. Many Protestant readers use it to teach that no human work can be the ground of standing right before God, which rests on Christ alone. Catholic and Orthodox readers affirm that salvation is by grace while giving more room to good works done in grace as truly pleasing to God. On any reading, the verse is a confession, not an accusation thrown at others. Those who say all their righteous acts are like filthy rags are including themselves.
passages.asks: The people ask God to tear open the heavens, and then admit why he seems far away. Ask what you would want God to come down and do. And ask whether you can say verse 6 about yourself without saying it first about someone else.

passages.t: Father and potter, and a burned temple
passages.happening:
‘But now, O LORD, You are our Father; we are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand’ (verse 8). ‘Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever’ (verse 9). They ask him to look on them, for they are all his people (verse 9).

‘Your holy cities have become a wilderness. Zion has become a wasteland and Jerusalem a desolation’ (verse 10). ‘Our holy and beautiful temple, where our fathers praised You, has been burned with fire, and all that was dear to us lies in ruins’ (verse 11).

The prayer ends with two questions. ‘After all this, O LORD, will You restrain Yourself? Will You keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The words But now turn the prayer. The people have confessed that they are unclean. Now they appeal to what God is to them: Father, and potter. Potters worked wet clay on a wheel in every town, and the picture of God shaping a person from clay goes back to the making of the man from dust. Clay cannot fix itself. Only the potter can.

The word all runs through the prayer: all their righteous acts, they all wither, they are all the work of God's hand, they are all his people. The same people who are all unclean are also all God's.

The burned temple matches what Nebuchadnezzar's commander Nebuzaradan did in 587 or 586 BC, when he burned the house of the LORD. Scholars who date these chapters after the return place the prayer before the second temple was finished around 515 BC. Those who read the whole book as Isaiah's take it as a prayer he gave for the generation that would see the ruin. It shares its mood with Lamentations and with Psalms 74 and 79.

The last question is left hanging on purpose. God's reply comes in chapter 65.
passages.later: Jeremiah watched a potter and heard God say, ‘Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel’ (Jeremiah 18:6). A psalm mourns the same ruin: ‘they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble’ (Psalm 79:1).
passages.asks: The people's only argument is that they are clay in God's hands and his people. Ask what you bring to God when you have nothing to offer but that. And ask whether you are willing to end a prayer with a question and wait for his answer.
